findings.claim: MCQ 'Which one of the following is the best example of a closed skill?' keys answer B and states 'All other options involve unpredictable, changing environments (open skills)'. Option D is 'A basketball player taking a free throw during a fast break'.
findings.truth: A basketball free throw is the textbook closed skill: play is stopped, the distance is fixed and no opponent can challenge. The same lesson's 4-mark question states that a free throw is a closed skill. The MCQ therefore has two correct options and marks a true answer wrong.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.1.1 (open/closed = predictability of environment); internal contradiction with lesson 1 practice question 4

findings.claim: Writing 'achievable' instead of 'accepted' is described as 'the most frequently penalised mistake'.
findings.truth: The spec lists 'accepted' as the A in SMART, but no published source ranks this as the most penalised error. The frequency claim is invented.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.1.2 SMART list; no mark-scheme source for the frequency claim

findings.claim: 'Mo Farah described being able to sense the precise moment his running economy started to drop in the final 200 m of a 5,000 m race.'
findings.truth: No such statement by Mo Farah exists. The sentence attributes an invented technical description to a named real athlete. The general point about elite intrinsic feedback stands without the attribution.
findings.evidence: no source for the quoted description

findings.claim: 'Knowledge of results (KR) ... is always extrinsic because the result is separate from the movement itself', repeated in a flashcard answered 'Yes'.
findings.truth: In motor-learning theory KR is normally classed as augmented (extrinsic) feedback, so the claim is defensible. But a performer who sees the ball go in the net gains outcome information from their own senses, and many GCSE resources allow intrinsic KR. The absolute 'always' overstates a contested point.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.1.4 names only intrinsic/extrinsic and KR/KP, without ruling on the overlap

findings.claim: 'too little causes under-performance through lethargy; too much causes over-performance through anxiety and loss of fine motor control.'
findings.truth: Over-arousal causes poor performance, not 'over-performance'. The sentence contradicts the inverted-U curve taught in the same lesson and would confuse a student revising the graph.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.1.5 (under or over arousal causing low performance levels)

findings.claim: 'When Beth Mead scored a hat-trick in England's opening game of the 2022 UEFA Women's Euros...'
findings.truth: Beth Mead scored the only goal in England's opening game against Austria on 6 July 2022 (1-0). Her hat-trick came in the third group game against Norway on 11 July 2022 (8-0).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Beth Mead (UEFA Women's Euro 2022 goals)

findings.truth: Sarah Storey has 19 Paralympic gold medals (30 medals in total) across nine Games from 1992 to 2024. The figure 17 was correct only up to Tokyo 2020.

findings.claim: Card 2 asks 'What does the media provide in the golden triangle?' and card 13 asks 'What does the media provide in the golden triangle relationship?'
findings.truth: The same question appears twice with near-identical answers, so the deck repeats itself. Not a factual error; the validator allows it because the answer strings differ.

findings.claim: 'One-sided answers are capped at the Developing band.'
findings.truth: No such cap exists. Extended answers are marked against level descriptors on the whole response; a specific invented capping rule tells a student something false about how they will be assessed.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section (Paper 2, extended answer questions); no published capping rule

findings.claim: 'A response that only condemns PED use without engaging with the arguments athletes make for using them will be capped at the Developing band.'
findings.truth: Same invented capping rule as F9. Balance is good advice, but the stated cap is not a real marking rule.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section; no published capping rule

findings.claim: Question 6 reads 'Describe two side effects of blood doping for a performer.' but carries a 3-mark tariff and a mark scheme that awards '1 mark each for any three distinct side effects' with a three-point model answer.
findings.truth: The question and its key disagree. A student who answers the question as written gives two side effects and can reach only 2 of the 3 marks. Asking for three side effects matches the tariff and the model answer.
findings.evidence: internal mismatch between question text, marks field and model answer

findings.claim: Knowledge check 1, 'What is home advantage in sport?', has correct index 2, which is the option 'A rule giving the home team extra time in finals'.
findings.truth: The correct option is index 1, 'The benefit gained from playing in a familiar venue with crowd support'. As keyed, the check marks the true answer wrong and teaches an invented rule about extra time.
findings.evidence: spec 3.2.2.3 (home-field advantage); lesson glossary definition of home advantage

findings.claim: 'a concept explored in the inverted-U theory covered in Lesson 10'
findings.truth: The inverted-U theory is Lesson 6 of this unit. Lesson 10 is Technology in Sport. The cross-reference sends a revising student to the wrong lesson.

findings.claim: 'Mental (serotonin, stress, emotional control) and social (teamwork, cooperation, socialisation) benefits carry equal mark-scheme weight.'
findings.truth: No published mark scheme assigns equal weight to the three wellbeing dimensions. Covering all three is sound advice, but the weighting claim is invented.

findings.claim: Flashcard answer: 'Mark schemes award equal weight to physical, mental and social benefits - ignoring one loses marks.'
findings.truth: Same invented weighting claim as F14, memorised as a fact through a flashcard.

findings.claim: 'Elite distance runners such as Dina Asher-Smith prepare for competition partly by ensuring glycogen stores are fully loaded...'
findings.truth: Dina Asher-Smith is a sprinter (100 m and 200 m), not a distance runner. The example also undercuts the point, because carbohydrate loading over several days is an endurance-event practice.
findings.evidence: Dina Asher-Smith competes at 100 m/200 m; spec 3.2.3.3 (carbohydrate as the main energy source)

findings.claim: 'For a sprint cyclist like Geraint Thomas, any cramping or slowing of reaction time in the final kilometre of a race could be decisive.'
findings.truth: Geraint Thomas is a road and stage-race cyclist (2018 Tour de France winner); his track career was in the team pursuit, an endurance event, not sprint cycling.
findings.evidence: Geraint Thomas's road and track record

findings.claim: A collapsible section teaches Hick's Law (reaction time increases with the number of possible responses).
findings.truth: Hick's Law is not on the 8582 spec; spec 3.2.1.3 requires only the basic information processing model. The content is accurate and clearly framed as an aside, so it misleads no one, but it is revision time spent off-spec.

findings.claim: The lesson presents 'Interpret Data' (4 marks) and 'Calculate from Data' (3 marks) as fixed exam question types, and states that the mark scheme 'typically awards 1 mark for correct working, 1 mark for the correct figure, and 1 mark for stating the unit', that missing a unit 'costs a mark', and that a bare comparison 'typically earns 1 mark'.
findings.truth: Paper 2 does contain data questions, but the spec publishes no fixed 'Interpret Data' or 'Calculate from Data' question type and no such mark split. These are this site's own practice-question labels presented to students as the real exam's structure. Two options: (a) leave it, because the advice itself (compare, calculate, explain, state units) is sound and touching it means rewriting both exam-tip paragraphs; (b) soften every reference to 'a data question' with no stated tariff or mark split. The same pattern appears in the data question labels used across the whole unit, so this is a subject-wide call, not a one-lesson fix.
findings.evidence: spec assessment section lines 304-321 (Paper 2 question types stated only as multiple choice/objective, short answer and extended answer); spec 3.1.4
findings.ruling: NOTE: house practice taxonomy labels (Interpret Data / Calculate from Data); advice sound, hedged; part of the subject-wide relabel sweep, not a one-lesson edit.

summary: Seventeen lessons checked against the AQA 8582 spec; sports psychology, socio-cultural and health content is largely accurate and every calculation in lessons 8, 13, 14, 16 and 17 recomputes correctly. Five hard errors matter: a knowledge check that marks the true definition of home advantage wrong, a closed-skill MCQ with two correct options, and three wrong facts about named athletes (Beth Mead's hat-trick, Sarah Storey's gold-medal total, Dina Asher-Smith called a distance runner).
